statement: One year after the congestion toll began, the share of storefronts vacant on 31 December 2025 in the Congestion Relief Zone had not risen relative to the rest of the city: the change from 31 December 2024, zone minus outside, is at most +0.5 percentage points and a rise of 1.2 points is excluded.

graph_evidence.concepts: congestion pricing, congestion charge, road pricing, cordon pricing, low emission zone | retail, restaurants, business
graph_evidence.summary: System Public Graph variable-name and concept searches (data/derived/congestion/graph_response_survival.json, section 'pricing'): no variable or concept for congestion pricing, cordon pricing, congestion relief zone or low emission zone; 'congestion charge' and 'road pricing' match only unrelated variables (hospital charges, an online market); 'traffic congestion' matches nine variables, none with a retail or business outcome. The graph supplies nothing on this link.

literature.citation: Quddus MA, Carmel A, Bell MGH (2007). The impact of the congestion charge on retail: the London experience. Journal of Transport Economics and Policy 41(1):113-133.
literature.finding: Cited from the registrant's memory, not re-read: sales at one Oxford Street department store fell after the 2003 charge, with no detectable effect on central London retail sales as a whole.

literature.citation: Daunfeldt S-O, Rudholm N, Ramme U (2009). Congestion charges and retail revenues: results from the Stockholm road pricing trial. Transportation Research Part A 43(3):306-309.
literature.finding: Cited from the registrant's memory, not re-read: no negative effect of the 2006 trial on retail revenue in shopping malls and shopping districts.

prediction.magnitude: DiD in percentage points of vacancy, 31 December 2025 against 31 December 2024, zone minus all other city ZIPs: between -1.5 and +0.5. The same DiD was -0.74, -1.40 and -0.45 in the three years to 2024 (the zone was recovering from its 2020 peak faster than the rest), so the expectation without any toll effect is about -0.5.
prediction.support_if: The DiD point estimate is at most +0.5 points AND the upper bound of its 95% bootstrap interval is below +1.2 points.
prediction.refute_if: The lower bound of the 95% bootstrap interval is above 0 (vacancy rose in the zone relative to outside).

plan: Data: Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not (92iy-9c3n). Script analyses/congestion/vacancy.py, written and run in design mode (years to 2024) before registration; design output data/derived/congestion/vacancy_design.json. Each reporting year gives vacant_on_12_31 for that 31 December; only the main annual filing (the filing_due_date with most rows) is used; rows answering neither YES nor NO are dropped. Areas by ZIP (analyses/congestion/common.py): zone = Manhattan south of 60th Street (about 15,100 storefronts in 2024, 12.3% vacant); comparison = all other city ZIPs (about 47,000, 7.3% vacant). Estimator: change in the vacancy share 2024 to 2025 in the zone minus the same change outside, in points. Interval: bootstrap over tax lots within each group, 2,000 draws, seed 20261113, percentiles. Can the test fail? The bootstrap se was 0.34 to 0.44 points in each earlier year and the DiD itself moved between -1.40 and -0.45 over 2022-24 (sd 0.49), so the uncertainty about the no-toll value is about 0.6 points around -0.5. A toll effect of +1.2 points (about 180 more vacant storefronts, a tenth more than now) would put the estimate near +0.7, two such standard errors from the no-effect expectation (D about 4); it would miss support_if (point estimate above +0.5, upper bound near +1.4) and would meet refute_if about half the time. A rise smaller than 1.2 points cannot be told from the trend, and the outcome will say so. Verdict by PRECEDENCE rules 1 and 2. Secondary, not deciding: the same DiD against Manhattan 60th-110th Street, against downtown Brooklyn with Long Island City, and against the rest of the city; the 2025 DiD minus the mean of the 2022-24 DiDs (a trend-adjusted figure). Limits known in advance: there is one observation after the toll; leases turn over slowly, so a year may be too soon; filings are by owners and coverage changed after 2020 (17,000 zone storefronts then, 15,100 now).
alternatives: Continued recovery of Manhattan retail from the pandemic peak in vacancy, which lowers zone vacancy whatever the toll does.
Office attendance and tourism in the zone, which changed in the same period.
Changes in which owners file, or in how vacancy is reported.
Commercial rents adjusting instead of vacancy.
data_seen_before_registration: 92iy-9c3n: row counts by reporting_year and filing_due_date for every year including 2025 and 2026 (counts only); two sample rows and the YES/NO totals for reporting year 2023; all rows for reporting years up to 2024 (design run).

No value of vacant_on_12_31 for reporting year 2025 or 2026 has been queried or seen. The registrant recalls press statements by the Governor's office in 2025-26 that retail activity in the zone rose, and none about the storefront registry.
